analysis.one_liner: Ends federal sugar price supports and quotas, but only once all countries drop their own sugar subsidies and tariffs.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by a single senator with zero cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing or vote, and the federal sugar program — which keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels — was left untouched.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have shut down the federal sugar program — government price support loans and production quotas for sugar beets and sugarcane — but only starting on the day the President certified that a global trade agreement (GATT) bans all sugar export subsidies, price supports, and import tariffs worldwide. Since no such worldwide ban exists, the condition would almost certainly never be met. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers and sugar-using food manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals, beverages), who pay noticeably more for sugar because federal price supports and import quotas keep domestic prices well above world prices. Taxpayers also benefit, since they cover losses when growers default on government sugar loans. The catch: under this bill's design, none of that would actually happen unless a worldwide ban on sugar tariffs and subsidies were certified — a condition no trade agreement has ever satisfied.

how_it_helps.text: It would repeal the sugar price support program (Section 206 of the Agricultural Act of 1949) and the sugar marketing quotas and acreage allotments, the two pillars that keep U.S. sugar prices above world levels for everyone who buys food.
It would bar the Secretary of Agriculture from ever providing price support for sugar beets or sugarcane again, and would end taxpayer-backed Commodity Credit Corporation lending for sugar.
It ties the termination to a worldwide agreement banning all sugar subsidies and tariffs, framed as a fair, reciprocal way to open the sugar market rather than a one-sided move.

analysis.who_pays: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and sugar processors, who would lose guaranteed price support loans and the quota system that shields them from competition. Any termination would be abrupt, with no transition assistance — the bill only requires settling loans already made.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sugar beet, cane growers and processors

drawbacks.text: The bill's trigger is almost certainly never going to fire: it takes effect only when a GATT agreement bans all sugar export subsidies, all price support and production adjustment programs, and all import tariffs worldwide — conditions no global trade agreement has ever met. Even if enacted, the bill would likely change nothing, making it a symbolic gesture rather than a working reform.

If the trigger ever were met, termination would be abrupt and unconditional: growers and processors would lose price supports and quota protections with no transition aid, and growers who had borrowed against supported prices would face the loss of that safety net (though outstanding government loans would still be settled).
Ending the program entirely could expose U.S. sugar buyers to swings in volatile world sugar prices in some years, the standard defense offered for keeping some form of price support.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — ending a program that transfers billions from food consumers to a few thousand sugar growers — is sound, and the bill would also stop taxpayer losses on sugar loans. But the bill is badly designed: by conditioning everything on a worldwide ban on sugar tariffs and subsidies that does not exist, it would not actually end the program even if passed. A serious reform would have set a direct termination date or phased out supports. As written, it was a statement of principle that sugar growers had no reason to fear, and they did not need to spend much effort stopping it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and not one cosponsor.

narrative.text: Sen. Spencer Abraham introduced the bill on October 25, 1995; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
Not a single senator from either party cosponsored it.
The Agriculture Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and the bill died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
Because the bill never passed, the sugar price support and quota programs it targeted remained in force, continuing to hold domestic sugar prices above world levels.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar growers and processors came out ahead: they kept the price supports and import quota system that hold U.S. sugar prices above world prices, while consumers and food manufacturers kept paying the difference.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers, who kept their price supports

for.name: Sen. Spencer Abraham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the sugar price support and quota programs, but could attract no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it died in committee at the end of the 104th Congress

against.name: Sugar grower and processor organizations
against.what_they_did: Have long lobbied to preserve the sugar price support and quota programs, which survived the 1995-96 farm bill debate intact

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; one Republican senator sponsored the bill and zero senators of either party cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors
industries.note: The bill would have ended the price support loans and production quotas that keep domestic sugar prices well above world prices — protections worth billions annually to a small, geographically concentrated group. Because the bill never advanced, they kept the program, and consumers kept paying above-world sugar prices.

industries.industry: Sugar-using food manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals, beverages)
industries.note: These firms buy sugar at U.S.-program prices far above world levels and pass the cost to shoppers; the bill would have removed the price floor and quota system once triggered. Its failure left their input costs — and consumers' grocery bills — unchanged.
